fields.title: The First Letter to Timothy
fields.subtitle: Pros Timotheon A, “First to Timothy”
fields.description: Paul’s letter to Timothy, his younger colleague, left behind in Ephesus to face teachers spreading “a different doctrine”: a charge to guard the gospel and to show how people ought to live in God’s household, “the church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth.” Paul tells of the mercy shown to him, the worst of sinners; asks for prayers for everyone, because God wants everyone to be saved; sets out what overseers and deacons must be; breaks into a hymn to Christ; urges Timothy to train himself in godliness and let no one look down on him for his youth; gives rules for widows, elders and slaves; and warns that the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Greek given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the letter’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the First Letter to Timothy?
qa.answer: A letter in the New Testament from the apostle Paul to Timothy, his trusted co-worker, whom he had left in Ephesus to stop false teachers and set the church in order (1:3). With 2 Timothy and Titus it is one of the three Pastoral Letters, so called because they concern the care of churches and their leaders. It covers sound teaching, prayer and worship, the qualities of overseers and deacons, the care of widows and elders, and the dangers of wealth.

qa.question: Who wrote 1 Timothy, and when?
qa.answer: The letter names Paul as its author, and the church received it as his from the second century. On that view it was written in the early or middle 60s AD, between an imprisonment in Rome that Paul was released from, as Eusebius records, and a second one. Since the nineteenth century many scholars have argued that the Pastoral Letters were written after Paul’s death by a follower, because of their vocabulary, church order and travels that are hard to fit into Acts; many others continue to defend Paul’s authorship.

qa.question: Who was Timothy?
qa.answer: A believer from Lystra, in what is now central Turkey, son of a Jewish mother and a Greek father (Acts 16:1), whose faith first lived in his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice (2 Timothy 1:5). Paul took him as a companion on his second journey, sent him to churches in Thessalonica, Corinth and Philippi, and named him as co-sender of six letters. Paul calls him “my true son in the faith” (1:2). Tradition remembers him as the first bishop of Ephesus.

qa.question: What does 1 Timothy 2:12 mean about women teaching?
qa.answer: The verse reads, “I do not allow a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; she is to remain quiet.” Christians understand it differently. Many churches take it as a lasting rule reserving the office of teaching and governing the church to men, grounded in the reasons Paul gives from Genesis (2:13–14). Others read it as Paul’s answer to a particular problem in Ephesus, where false teachers had influenced some women, noting that the rare Greek verb may mean to domineer and that women such as Priscilla and Phoebe taught and served in Paul’s churches. All agree that the passage begins by saying that a woman should learn.

qa.question: Does the Bible say money is the root of all evil?
qa.answer: Not quite. 1 Timothy 6:10 says, “the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil.” It is the love of money, not money itself, and the Greek has no article before “root”: every kind of evil can grow from it. The same chapter calls godliness with contentment great gain, and tells the rich not to trust in wealth but to be generous, so that they may “take hold of the life that is truly life” (6:19).

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Greek beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
Here is a saying you can rely on, which deserves to be fully accepted: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, and I am the worst of them. But I was shown mercy for this very reason: so that in me, the worst of all, Christ Jesus could show how completely patient he is, as an example for those who would come to believe in him and receive eternal life.

— 1 Timothy 1:15–16

Most of Paul’s letters were written to churches. This one is written to a man: Timothy, his younger colleague, whom he had left behind in Ephesus to deal with a church in trouble. Teachers there were spreading “a different doctrine”, arguing over myths and family trees, forbidding marriage and certain foods. Timothy was young, perhaps timid, and often unwell. Paul writes to tell him how people ought to live “in God’s household, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth.”

Together with 2 Timothy and Titus, this letter has been called one of the Pastoral Letters since the eighteenth century, because all three concern the care of churches and those who lead them. They have shaped Christian thinking about ministry more than any other part of the New Testament.

Timothy

Timothy came from Lystra, in what is now central Turkey. His mother was a Jewish believer and his father a Greek (Acts 16:1). Paul took him on as a companion on his second journey, and from then on Timothy appears everywhere: in Thessalonica, Corinth, Philippi and Ephesus, and as co-sender of six of Paul’s letters. Paul trusted him like no one else. “I have no one else of the same heart,” he told the Philippians (2:20). In this letter he calls him “my true son in the faith”.

Ephesus was the greatest city of the province of Asia, home of the vast temple of Artemis. Paul had spent more than two years there, and the church had spread through the region (Acts 19:10). Before he left, he had warned its elders that savage wolves would come in among them, and that some of their own would distort the truth (Acts 20:29–30). That is the situation this letter addresses.

Who wrote the Pastoral Letters?

The letter opens “From Paul”, and for most of Christian history that settled the question. Since the nineteenth century many scholars have argued that the Pastoral Letters were written after Paul’s death by a follower writing in his name. They point to a vocabulary different from Paul’s other letters, a more settled church order, and travels that are hard to fit into Acts.

Others, including many scholars today, hold that Paul wrote them, perhaps with more freedom given to a secretary, late in his life. They note that the letters are full of personal detail, and that the church historian Eusebius records a tradition that Paul was released from his first imprisonment in Rome, worked again in the east, and was imprisoned a second time. On that view 1 Timothy was written in the early or middle 60s. Readers on both sides agree that these letters carry the voice of Paul’s teaching to the next generation, and the church has read them as Scripture from the second century on.

The shape of the letter

  • Chapter 1: sound teaching and the grace that saved Paul. A charge to stop the false teachers, and Paul’s own story.
  • Chapter 2: prayer and worship. Prayers for everyone, and how men and women are to conduct themselves when the church gathers.
  • Chapter 3: leaders. What overseers and deacons must be, and a hymn to Christ.
  • Chapter 4: Timothy’s own life and teaching. False asceticism refused, and godliness trained.
  • Chapters 5–6: the household of God. Older and younger, widows, elders, slaves and masters, the danger of money, and a closing charge.

The worst of sinners

Before he gives Timothy a single instruction about the church, Paul tells his own story. He was once a man who spoke against Christ and persecuted his people. He was shown mercy. And he sums up the whole gospel in a saying he calls one “you can rely on”: “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, and I am the worst of them.” If Christ could be so patient with Paul, no one is beyond his reach.

The verse has a long history of its own. In Cambridge, a few years after 1516, a young scholar named Thomas Bilney, reading Erasmus’s new Greek and Latin New Testament, came upon these words and found, he later wrote, that his bruised bones leapt for joy. Through Bilney, Hugh Latimer was won to the Reformation, and both men later died at the stake. John Bunyan took his own title, Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners, from the same verse in the older English Bible.

Prayer for everyone

The first thing Paul asks of the church is prayer: for everyone, including kings and all who hold high office. The reason is God himself, who “wants everyone to be saved and to come to know the truth”:

For there is one God, and one mediator between God and humanity, Christ Jesus, himself human, who gave himself as a ransom for all. This was the testimony given at the right time.

— 1 Timothy 2:5–6

Christians have debated how to hold together God’s will that all be saved and his choice of some; Calvin, preaching on this passage, read “everyone” as all kinds and conditions of people, while Wesley and many others read it as every person without exception. Both agreed on what follows from it: the church must pray for all and preach to all.

Men and women in worship

Paul asks men to pray without anger or quarrelling, and women to adorn themselves not with braided hair and gold but with good works. Then come two verses that have been argued over more than almost any in the New Testament: “A woman should learn quietly and with full submission. I do not allow a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; she is to remain quiet.” Paul gives a reason from Genesis, from the order of creation and the deception of Eve.

Christians read these words in different ways. Many churches, Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant, take them as a lasting rule that the ordained office of teaching and governing the church belongs to men. Others, noting that the rare Greek verb for “exercise authority” may mean to domineer, and that false teachers in Ephesus had made inroads among some women (5:13–15; 2 Timothy 3:6–7), read them as Paul’s answer to a particular situation, and point to women such as Priscilla, Phoebe and Junia who taught and served in his churches. Readers on every side should notice that the first command is that a woman should learn, a striking thing to say in the ancient world. The puzzling promise that “she will be saved through childbearing” (2:15) has no agreed explanation.

Overseers and deacons

Chapter 3 lists what a church’s leaders must be. The overseer (in Greek episkopos, from which “bishop” comes) must be “faithful to his one wife, clear-headed, self-controlled, respected, welcoming to guests, able to teach”. Almost every quality is one any Christian should have; what stands out is how little is said about talent and how much about character, home and reputation. Deacons must be tested first, and “the women likewise” must be worthy of respect, either deacons’ wives or women who served as deacons, as Phoebe did (Romans 16:1).

Then, at the centre of the letter, Paul breaks into what looks like an early Christian hymn:

Beyond all question, the mystery of our faith is great: He was revealed in a human body, vindicated by the Spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among the nations, believed in throughout the world, taken up in glory.

— 1 Timothy 3:16

The church’s order matters because the church holds this truth. Its leaders are chosen with care because of who it is they serve.

Train yourself in godliness

The false teachers forbade marriage and certain foods. Paul answers that “everything God created is good, and nothing should be refused if it is received with thanks.” The discipline he wants is of another kind: “Train yourself in godliness.” The word godliness runs through the letter. It means a life shaped through and through by reverence for God, and it has to be practised, as an athlete trains. Then he speaks to Timothy himself:

Do not let anyone look down on you because you are young, but set the believers an example in how you speak and live, in love, in faith and in purity.

— 1 Timothy 4:12

Read Scripture to the church, preach, teach, use your gift, and “keep a close watch on yourself and on your teaching.”

The household of God

Chapter 5 treats the church as a family: older men as fathers, younger men as brothers, older women as mothers, younger women as sisters. It gives careful rules for supporting widows who have no one else, urges families to care for their own, and tells Timothy to honour elders who lead well, pay those who preach and teach, and never accept an accusation against one without witnesses. There are instructions for slaves, written within an institution the letter does not directly challenge, which remind believing slaves that their believing masters are “brothers and sisters” and “dear to them”.

Godliness and gain

Some of the false teachers treated religion as a way to make money. Paul turns the idea around:

Godliness is indeed great gain, when it comes with contentment. For we brought nothing into the world, and we can take nothing out of it.

— 1 Timothy 6:6–7

Then come the words so often misquoted. Not money but “the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil”, and those eager for it have “pierced themselves with many griefs”. To the rich he gives not condemnation but a charge: to put their hope in God, “who richly gives us everything to enjoy”, to be rich in good deeds, and so to “take hold of the life that is truly life.” The letter ends as it began, with Timothy told to guard what has been entrusted to him.

How to read 1 Timothy

Read it as a letter between friends, an older man to a younger one he loves, not as a church manual. Notice the outbursts of praise (1:17; 3:16; 6:15–16): even its instructions are written by someone overwhelmed by God. Notice the five sayings in these letters introduced as trustworthy (1:15; 3:1; 4:9; 2 Timothy 2:11; Titus 3:8), short sayings the churches already knew. And on the hardest passages, read slowly, read the whole letter around them, and read with charity toward those who understand them differently.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and given freely to the public domain. It is printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. A few of its choices in 1 Timothy are worth knowing about before you begin.

“He was revealed in a human body” (3:16). Many later manuscripts read “God was revealed in the flesh”, the wording of older English Bibles. The earliest manuscripts read “who”, which in early Greek writing differs from “God” by two small strokes. This translation follows them, and begins the line “He”. The line still speaks of Christ.

“Faithful to his one wife” (3:2, 3:12). The Greek is literally “a one-woman man”. It may mean faithful in marriage, married only once, or not having more than one wife. The translation takes the first sense.

“To exercise authority” (2:12). The Greek verb occurs only here in the New Testament. The translation gives its usual sense, while its notes record that it can also mean to domineer.

“A root of all kinds of evil” (6:10). There is no article before “root” in the Greek, and the translation does not supply one: Paul is not saying every evil comes from the love of money, but that every kind can grow from it.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Greek beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: 1 Timothy 1
fields.body_html:
Greeting

From Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the command of God our Savior and of Christ Jesus our hope, to Timothy, my true son in the faith. Grace, mercy and peace to you from God the Father and from Christ Jesus our Lord.

Warning against a different doctrine

When I was leaving for Macedonia, I urged you to stay on in Ephesus, so that you could order certain people to stop teaching a different doctrine and to stop giving their minds to myths and endless lists of ancestors. These lead to speculation rather than to God’s plan, which works through faith. The aim of our instruction is love that comes from a pure heart, a good conscience and a faith without pretense. Some have missed this aim and wandered off into empty talk. They want to be teachers of the law, but they do not understand what they are saying, or the things they are so sure about.

What the law is for

We know that the law is good, if it is used as it should be. We know that law is not made for people who do right, but for the lawless and the rebellious, the ungodly and sinners, those who have no regard for what is holy, those who kill their fathers or mothers, murderers, the sexually immoral, men who have sex with men, slave traders, liars, those who break their oaths, and whatever else goes against the sound teaching that agrees with the glorious gospel of the blessed God, which has been entrusted to me.

Mercy for the worst of sinners

I thank Christ Jesus our Lord, who has given me strength, because he judged me trustworthy and appointed me to serve him, even though I used to speak against him, persecute his people and treat them violently. But I was shown mercy, because I did not know what I was doing in my unbelief, and the grace of our Lord poured over me, along with the faith and love that are found in Christ Jesus. Here is a saying you can rely on, which deserves to be fully accepted: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, and I am the worst of them. But I was shown mercy for this very reason: so that in me, the worst of all, Christ Jesus could show how completely patient he is, as an example for those who would come to believe in him and receive eternal life. To the King of all ages, the immortal, invisible and only God, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

Timothy’s charge

Timothy, my son, I am entrusting you with this charge, in keeping with the prophecies once spoken over you, so that by following them you may fight the good fight, holding on to faith and a good conscience. Some have thrown their conscience aside, and their faith has been wrecked. Among them are Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I have handed over to Satan so that they may learn not to blaspheme.

fields.title: 1 Timothy 2
fields.body_html:
Prayer for all, and the one mediator

First of all, then, I urge that requests, prayers, intercessions and thanks be offered for everyone: for kings and for all who hold high office, so that we may live peaceful and quiet lives, fully devoted to God and worthy of respect. This is good, and it pleases God our Savior, who wants everyone to be saved and to come to know the truth. For there is one God, and one mediator between God and humanity, Christ Jesus, himself human, who gave himself as a ransom for all. This was the testimony given at the right time. For this purpose I was appointed a preacher and an apostle (I am telling the truth; I am not lying), a teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth.

Instructions for men and women

So I want the men everywhere to pray, lifting up holy hands, free from anger and quarreling. In the same way, I want women to dress in a fitting way, with modesty and good sense, and not to make braided hair, gold, pearls or costly clothes their adornment, but good works, as is right for women who claim to honor God. A woman should learn quietly and with full submission. I do not allow a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; she is to remain quiet. For Adam was formed first, and then Eve. And Adam was not the one deceived; it was the woman who was deceived and fell into sin. Yet she will be saved through childbearing, if they continue in faith, love and holiness, with self-control.

fields.title: 1 Timothy 3
fields.body_html:
What an overseer must be

Here is a saying you can rely on: anyone who wants to be an overseer is setting their heart on a good work. So an overseer must be someone no one can fairly criticize: faithful to his one wife, clear-headed, self-controlled, respected, welcoming to guests, able to teach, not a heavy drinker, not violent but gentle, not quarrelsome, not someone who loves money. He must manage his own household well and see that his children obey him and are respectful in every way. (If someone does not know how to manage his own household, how can he take care of God’s church?) He must not be a recent convert, or he may become proud and fall under the same judgment as the devil. He must also be well thought of by outsiders, so that he does not fall into disgrace and into the devil’s trap.

Deacons

In the same way, deacons must be worthy of respect, sincere in what they say, not heavy drinkers, and not greedy for money. They must hold on to the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience. They too should first be tested; then, if no charge can be brought against them, let them serve. The women likewise must be worthy of respect, not slanderers, clear-headed and trustworthy in everything. A deacon must be faithful to his one wife and manage his children and household well. Those who serve well earn a good standing for themselves and great boldness in their faith in Christ Jesus.

The mystery of our faith

I am writing you these things, though I hope to come to you soon, so that, if I am delayed, you will know how people ought to live in God’s household, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth. Beyond all question, the mystery of our faith is great: He was revealed in a human body, vindicated by the Spirit, seen by angels, proclaimed among the nations, believed in throughout the world, taken up in glory.

fields.title: 1 Timothy 4
fields.body_html:
Some will abandon the faith

The Spirit says clearly that in later times some will abandon the faith and follow deceiving spirits and things taught by demons. Such teaching comes through hypocritical liars whose consciences have been branded as with a hot iron. They forbid people to marry and order them to keep away from certain foods, which God created to be received with thanks by those who believe and know the truth. For everything God created is good, and nothing should be refused if it is received with thanks, because it is made holy by God’s word and by prayer.

Train yourself in godliness

If you teach these things to the brothers and sisters, you will be a good servant of Christ Jesus, feeding yourself on the words of the faith and of the good teaching you have followed. Have nothing to do with godless and silly myths. Instead, train yourself in godliness. Physical training has some value, but godliness is valuable in every way, since it holds promise both for life now and for the life to come. Here is a saying you can rely on, which deserves to be fully accepted. This is why we work hard and endure insults: we have put our hope in the living God, the Savior of all people, and especially of those who believe.

Set the believers an example

Give these instructions, and teach them. Do not let anyone look down on you because you are young, but set the believers an example in how you speak and live, in love, in faith and in purity. Until I come, devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture, to preaching and to teaching. Do not neglect the gift that is in you, which was given to you through a prophetic word when the elders laid their hands on you. Put these things into practice and give yourself wholly to them, so that everyone may see your progress. Keep a close watch on yourself and on your teaching. Persevere in them, for if you do, you will save both yourself and your hearers.

fields.title: 1 Timothy 5
fields.body_html:
Older and younger believers

Never speak harshly to an older man, but appeal to him as you would to a father. Treat younger men as brothers, older women as mothers, and younger women as sisters, with complete purity.

Caring for widows

Give honor and support to widows who are really in need. But if a widow has children or grandchildren, they should first learn to put their faith into practice by caring for their own family, and so repay their parents and grandparents, for this pleases God. The widow who is really in need, left all alone, has put her hope in God and keeps praying and asking for help night and day. But the widow who lives for pleasure is dead even while she is alive. Give these instructions as well, so that no one may be open to blame. Anyone who does not provide for their relatives, and especially for their own household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.

The list of widows

No widow should be put on the list unless she is over sixty and has been faithful to her husband. She must be well known for good deeds: bringing up children, welcoming strangers, washing the feet of God’s people, helping those in trouble, and giving herself to every kind of good work. But do not put younger widows on the list. When their desires pull them away from Christ, they want to marry, and so they come under judgment for breaking their first pledge. Besides, they get into the habit of being idle, going from house to house; and not only idle, but gossips and busybodies, talking about things they should not. So I want the younger widows to marry, have children and manage their homes, giving the enemy no opportunity to speak evil of us. Some have already turned away to follow Satan. If a believing woman has widows in her family, she should help them and not let the church be burdened, so that the church can help the widows who are really in need.

Instructions about elders

Elders who lead the church well should be thought worthy of double honor, especially those who work hard at preaching and teaching. For the Scripture says, “Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain,” and “The worker deserves to be paid.” Do not listen to an accusation against an elder unless it is supported by two or three witnesses. Those who keep on sinning should be rebuked in front of everyone, so that the others will also take warning. In the presence of God and Christ Jesus and the chosen angels, I solemnly charge you to keep these instructions without prejudging anyone and to do nothing out of favoritism. Do not be in a hurry to lay hands on anyone, and do not share in other people’s sins. Keep yourself pure. Stop drinking only water, and take a little wine for your stomach and your frequent illnesses.

Some people’s sins are obvious, going ahead of them to judgment; the sins of others show up later. In the same way, good deeds are obvious, and even those that are not cannot stay hidden.

fields.title: 1 Timothy 6
fields.body_html:
Slaves and their masters

All who are under the yoke of slavery should count their masters worthy of full respect, so that God’s name and our teaching are not spoken against. Those whose masters are believers must not look down on them because they are brothers and sisters. Instead, they should serve them all the more, because those who benefit from their good service are fellow believers and dear to them.

False teaching and the love of money

Teach these things and urge them on people. Anyone who teaches something different and does not agree with the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and with teaching that leads to godliness is puffed up with pride and understands nothing. Such people have an unhealthy appetite for controversy and arguments about words. These lead to envy, quarreling, slander and evil suspicions, and to constant friction between people whose minds are corrupted and who have lost hold of the truth. They think godliness is a way to make money. Godliness is indeed great gain, when it comes with contentment. For we brought nothing into the world, and we can take nothing out of it. If we have food and clothing, we will be content with that. Those who want to get rich fall into temptation and a trap, and into many foolish and harmful desires that drag people down into ruin and destruction. For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. Some people, eager for money, have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many griefs.

Man of God, compete well

But you, man of God, run from all this, and pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, endurance and gentleness. Compete well in the good contest of the faith. Take hold of the eternal life to which you were called when you made your good confession in front of many witnesses. In the presence of God, who gives life to everything, and of Christ Jesus, who made the good confession when he testified before Pontius Pilate, I charge you to keep this command without fault or blame until our Lord Jesus Christ appears. God will bring this about at the right time: the blessed and only Ruler, the King of kings and Lord of lords, who alone is immortal, who lives in light no one can approach, whom no one has seen or can see. To him be honor and eternal power. Amen.

Instructions for the rich

Tell those who are rich in this present world not to be proud and not to put their hope in wealth, which is so uncertain, but in God, who richly gives us everything to enjoy. Tell them to do good, to be rich in good deeds, to give generously and to share. In this way they will store up treasure for themselves as a firm foundation for the age to come, so that they may take hold of the life that is truly life.

Guard what has been entrusted to you

Timothy, guard what has been entrusted to you. Turn away from godless, empty chatter and the contradictions of what is wrongly called knowledge. Some have claimed it, and in doing so have strayed from the faith.

Grace be with you all.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
Timothy, guard what has been entrusted to you. Turn away from godless, empty chatter and the contradictions of what is wrongly called knowledge. Some have claimed it, and in doing so have strayed from the faith.

— 1 Timothy 6:20–21

The letter ends with one word of command: guard. Timothy has been given something that is not his own, the gospel, the “sound teaching” that agrees with “the glorious gospel of the blessed God”, and his task is to keep it safe and hand it on whole. Everything else in the letter, the prayers, the qualifications for leaders, the care of widows, the warnings about money, serves that one charge.

The question the letter leaves

What does a healthy church look like? 1 Timothy answers in an unexpected way. It says little about programmes or growth or eloquence. It talks about character: leaders who are self-controlled, gentle and faithful at home; members who pray for everyone, care for their own families, honour the old and protect the vulnerable; a community content with food and clothing and generous with everything else. And it talks about truth: teaching that is sound, that is, healthy, because it leads to “love that comes from a pure heart, a good conscience and a faith without pretense.”

That aim, stated in the first chapter, is the test of every other instruction. Teaching that produces quarrels, pride and greed has missed it, however clever. Teaching that produces love has not.

And at the centre of it all stands not a rule but a person: Christ Jesus, the one mediator, who “came into the world to save sinners”. A church that forgets the mercy shown to the worst of them has forgotten why it exists.

Where to go from here

For nearly two thousand years pastors have gone back to this letter to learn their work, and many of the best of them are in this library:

  • On mercy to the worst of sinners (1:15). John Bunyan’s Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners, whose title comes from this verse.
  • On prayer for all and the one mediator (2:1–7). John Calvin’s sermon God Will Have All Men to Be Saved, on 2:3–5.
  • On the mystery of our faith (3:16). Calvin’s sermon The Mystery of Godliness.
  • On the work of a pastor (3:1–7; 4:16; 5:22). Gregory the Great’s The Book of Pastoral Rule, which weighs Paul’s words on those who want to be overseers; John Chrysostom’s On the Priesthood; Richard Baxter’s The Reformed Pastor, on Paul’s charge to the elders of Ephesus (Acts 20:28); and Charles H. Spurgeon’s Lectures to My Students, whose lecture “The Minister’s Self-Watch” takes 4:16 as its text.
  • On contentment and wealth (6:6–19). John Henry Newman’s sermon Temporal Advantages (6:7–8); Chrysostom’s Homily II on the Statues, preached in a terrified Antioch on the charge to the rich (6:17); Thomas Watson’s The Art of Divine Contentment; and Clement of Alexandria’s Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?
  • The church of the next generation. The Epistle and Martyrdom of Polycarp, in which Polycarp echoes this letter on the love of money, and Ignatius of Antioch’s letter to the church at Ephesus, in The Epistles of Ignatius and His Life’s Story.

Then read 2 Timothy, in this same edition: Paul’s last letter to the same young man, written from prison.

You can also go the other way, from the text to the classics. Every reference to 1 Timothy in this library can be tapped to read the verse, and the Scripture pages gather, chapter by chapter, what the great writers of the church have said about each passage of this letter.

But the best next step may be to read the letter again, and to notice how often its instructions give way to worship. Paul cannot speak about the church for long without speaking of the God it belongs to:

To the King of all ages, the immortal, invisible and only God, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

— 1 Timothy 1:17
